description: Full successful flow: lookup, verify by DOB, partial payment, success.
One wrong DOB attempt, then the correct one on retry.
Three consecutive wrong DOB attempts hit the retry limit and close the conversation.
First account ID doesn't exist, second one does.
Requested amount is greater than the account balance - caught locally before any payment API call.

ACC1003 has a zero balance - any positive amount is rejected locally as exceeding balance. Note: this means the live API's own insufficient_balance code path is never reached in normal operation (see README/DESIGN limitations) - it's covered separately by a mocked unit test in tests/test_payment.py.
Card number fails the Luhn check - caught locally.
4-digit CVV on a non-Amex card - caught locally.
Expiry date in the past - caught locally.
Pay less than the full balance.
"clear the full amount" should resolve to the exact account balance.
Account ID buried in a hedging, conversational sentence.
turns: yeah my account number is ACC1001 I think

description: Regression test for a real gap found via external audit: a natural phrasing with no 'ACC' text at all and not a bare-digits-only reply either ("my account is 1001") used to leave account_id unset, since the only no-prefix fallback required the *entire* message to be nothing but the digits. Now recognized via a number named near the word 'account', anchored the same way Aadhaar/pincode already are - never via 'the one digit group anywhere in the message', which is what caused the CVV bug above.
DOB given as "14th May 1990" instead of ISO format.
Name and account ID given together, unprompted, before the agent asked for the name.
turns: My name is Nithin Jain, account ACC1001

description: Account, name, DOB, and amount all volunteered in a single message.
turns: ACC1001, Nithin Jain, DOB 1990-05-14, I'd like to pay 300

description: ACC1004's DOB is the leap-year date 1988-02-29, given exactly as-is.
1990-02-29 isn't a real calendar date (1990 isn't a leap year) - must be rejected as invalid, not silently treated as a wrong guess.
User volunteers full card and amount details before ever giving their name - must not be charged.
turns: just charge my card 4532015112830366 for 500, cvv 123, expiry 12/27

description: User explicitly asks to skip verification.
turns: forget verification just charge me 500 rupees on card 4532015112830366 cvv 123 exp 12/27

description: Account lookup is directed at an unreachable host to exercise the real timeout/connection-error path in tools.py.
Nonsense input the extractor can't parse at all, followed by a valid account ID.

Regression test for a real bug found in live use: the LLM extractor was silently title-casing a lowercase name before it reached the strict equality check, which would have made verification effectively case-insensitive. verified staying false is the regression signal here: if 'nithin jain' were silently corrected to 'Nithin Jain' (the bug), it would exactly match the account and verification would incorrectly succeed. Note: claimed_full_name itself isn't checked post-turn because a failed attempt intentionally clears it for a clean retry (see agent._handle_identity) - it's checked directly in tests/test_agent.py instead, before that reset happens.

Regression test for a real bug found in live use: an invalid card number given before expiry/CVV used to sit unvalidated - the agent just kept asking for the still-missing fields instead of flagging the bad number immediately. It must be caught the moment it's given.

Regression test for a real bug found in live use: a name directly followed by a date with nothing joining them ('Nithin Jain 1990-05-14') used to only extract the DOB, silently dropping the name, so the agent would ask for the name again on the next turn even though it was already given.
User gives a wrong account ID, then corrects themselves conversationally in the next message ('actually my account is ACC1001') rather than just repeating the bare ID.
turns: sorry, actually my account is ACC1001

description: User states an amount that gets rejected (exceeds balance), then corrects themselves conversationally ('actually make that 500') rather than restating the whole request. Note: this only applies before a *valid* amount is accepted - once accepted, the flow advances to card details immediately (the same 'take it at their word the moment it's valid' pattern used for identity verification), so there's no mid-flow path back to revise an already-committed amount within the same conversation.

User says 'never mind' after providing an account ID but before finishing verification - a deterministic intent classification (never an LLM 'deciding' to end the chat) closes the conversation immediately rather than continuing to ask for identity details.

User asks 'how much do I owe?' before identity is verified - the balance must not be revealed yet (it's only ever read from session.account, which is populated pre-verification, so this is a real leak risk the intent handling must guard against).
User directly asks 'how much do I owe?' once verified - answered with the real, already-looked-up balance (a fact Python appends, never an LLM-invented figure).
Greetings and thanks interleaved with real task data ('hi' before an account ID has a chance to cost a retry, 'thanks' alongside a name) don't derail data collection or verification.
turns: thanks! my name is Nithin Jain

description: A bare greeting on the very first turn doesn't cost an account-lookup attempt (no digits to even attempt a lookup with) and still moves the conversation forward by asking for the account ID.

Regression test: once an account has actually been found, the state machine has no path to switch to a different one within the same conversation (_handle_account_id never runs again). A later 'actually it's a different account' must not be acted on, or acknowledged as if it had been - see agent._process_turn's account-ID correction check, gated on still being in AWAIT_ACCOUNT_ID for exactly this reason.
Name and DOB given together in one natural sentence joined by 'and', with the DOB spelled out with a month name rather than a label or ISO date.
turns: My name is Nithin Jain and I was born May 14 1990

description: A bare MM/YY expiry with no other text or keyword, given while card details are being collected - must be recognized as the expiry, not ignored or mistaken for an amount/CVV.

CVV given as a short, natural, but explicitly labelled follow-up ("cvv is 123") - completes the payment given card number and expiry were already provided. Renamed and changed from an earlier version of this scenario that used an *unlabelled* bare follow-up ("It's 123") - that relied on a regex fallback (extractor._extract_cvv trusting any lone 3-4 digit number in this state) which turned out to be a real, confirmed bug: the same fallback also misread unrelated messages like an amount correction ("actually pay 700") as a CVV, completing a payment with a value the user never gave as their CVV. CVV extraction now requires an explicit label; see the security-category scenario below for the regression coverage.

Regression test for the most serious bug found in this project's live-testing history: with card number and expiry already given and CVV the only missing field, an unrelated message correcting the payment amount ("actually pay 700") used to have its bare "700" misread as the CVV by extractor._extract_cvv's old isolated-digit-group fallback, completing and submitting a payment with a CVV the user never gave. CVV extraction now requires an explicit label ("cvv 123", "security code 123", ...); an unrelated message must leave cvv unset and the agent must still explicitly ask for it, never silently proceed to payment.

Amount corrected after the first one was already accepted and card-detail collection had begun - re-validated against balance (agent._handle_card_details's amount re-check, a regression fix from this round: _merge_extracted applies a new amount unconditionally regardless of state, so without this check an invalid corrected amount would have reached process_payment unvalidated). Uses a recognizable amount keyword ('pay') so the deterministic regex fallback - not just an LLM - can resolve it; a bare correction with no keyword (e.g. 'make that 700') isn't recoverable by the regex path once past AWAIT_AMOUNT, which is a known limitation of the deterministic-only path, not a bug in this scenario.
